readerTitle: Same price rise, different reaction: why the reason matters more than the number
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler, 1986 공정성 설문) + 가상 사례 (배관 업체, 사내 데이터 플랫폼 팀)
insight: 고객은 가격의 크기보다 가격이 오른 이유를 판단한다. 비용이 올라서 올리면 받아들이고, 고객의 급한 사정을 이용해 올리면 벌한다.
misconception: 고객이 화내는 건 가격이 많이 올랐기 때문이다. 인상 폭만 작게 하면 괜찮다.

sources.text: Kahneman, D., Knetsch, J. L., & Thaler, R. (1986). Fairness as a Constraint on Profit Seeking: Entitlements in the Market. American Economic Review, 76(4), 728–741.
배관 업체와 사내 데이터 플랫폼 팀 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 눈삽 문항: 눈보라 다음 날 아침 철물점이 눈삽 가격을 $15에서 $20로 올림 → 응답자 82%가 불공정(Unfair 또는 Very unfair)으로 평가. 원문 Table/문항 1의 수치를 게시 전 다시 확인하세요.
양상추 문항: 운송 문제로 도매가가 포기당 30센트 오르자 식료품점이 소매가를 30센트 올림 → 79% 수용, 21% 불공정. 원문 수치 재확인 필요.
자동차 딜러 문항: 인기 모델 품귀 시 정가보다 $200 더 받음 → 71% 불공정, 정가보다 $200 할인하던 것을 정가로 되돌림 → 42% 불공정. 원문 문항 2A/2B 수치 재확인 필요.
설문은 1984~1985년경 캐나다 토론토·밴쿠버 주민 대상 전화 설문으로 알려져 있습니다. 카드에는 'people in Canada'로만 적었습니다. 지역과 연도를 원문으로 확인하세요.
가상 사례 계산: 배관 출장비 $90 → $150는 $60 인상(약 67%). 사내 팀: 벤더 라이선스 25% 인상, 사용자당 월 $40 → $50.

cards.title: Same $60 rise. One plumber gets thanked, the other gets one-star reviews.
body: Two plumbers in the same town both raise their call-out fee from $90 to $150.
One does it the week a freeze bursts pipes across town. The other does it after his insurance and van costs jump. Customers shrug at the second and punish the first.
The number is identical. The story behind it is not.

image.label: Two identical price tags, one with angry faces, one with calm faces
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 배관공 밴 두 대가 나란히 있고 둘 다 "$150" 가격표. 왼쪽 밴 위에는 눈송이와 화난 말풍선, 오른쪽 밴 위에는 영수증 아이콘과 고개를 끄덕이는 말풍선. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: A cold snap triples your calls.
body: You run a small plumbing company. A freeze hits and calls triple overnight. Your crew is working long shifts, and you could easily charge more.
What do you do with your prices this week?

options.text: Raise the standard rate 50% while demand lasts
options.feedback: You earn more this week, but customers read it as profiting from their emergency. Many will remember your name for the wrong reason.

options.text: Keep the standard rate, and apply your usual after-hours rate, which was posted all year, to night calls
options.feedback: You still earn more for overtime work, and the rule existed before the crisis. It looks like a cost you're covering, not a moment you're exploiting.

options.text: Keep prices, but add a new "high-demand surcharge" line to every bill
options.feedback: Smaller than option A, but the label says exactly what customers resent: you're charging more because they need you.

cards.title: Same kind of rise. Very different verdicts.
body: In a classic 1986 study, Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch and Richard Thaler asked people in Canada to judge everyday price changes.
A hardware store raises snow shovels from $15 to $20 the morning after a snowstorm. A grocer raises lettuce by 30 cents after its own wholesale cost rises 30 cents.

rows.label: Lettuce, after the grocer's cost rose

cards.callout: Both are price rises. Only one looked like taking advantage.

image.label: Same kind of rise. Very different verdicts.
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: Perceived fairness
body: **Perceived fairness** is the customer's judgment of *why* a price changed, not just how much.

People carry a reference price, the price they're used to. They accept that a business may protect its normal profit, so passing on a real cost rise feels fair. Raising prices because buyers suddenly need you more feels unfair, even when it's legal and the market would bear it.
The researchers called this a dual entitlement: the customer is entitled to the usual price, and the seller to its usual profit.

image.label: Scale weighing 'my costs went up' against 'you need me now'
image.brief: 저울 일러스트. 왼쪽 접시에 "My costs went up" 라벨과 영수증, 오른쪽 접시에 "You need me now" 라벨과 눈보라. 왼쪽 위에 초록 체크, 오른쪽 위에 빨간 X.

cards.title: The same $200 can be fair or unfair.
body: The same study described a car dealer facing a shortage of a popular model.
When the dealer charged $200 *above* list price, 71% called it unfair. When a dealer who had been giving $200 *off* list simply stopped the discount, only 42% did.
Customers paid the same amount either way. Losing a discount felt like returning to normal. A new premium felt like being squeezed.

image.label: Two arrows reaching the same price from different starting points
image.brief: 가격 축 위에 화살표 두 개. 하나는 "List price"에서 위로 "+$200", 하나는 "−$200" 위치에서 "List price"로 올라옴. 둘 다 같은 높이에 도달하지만 첫 번째에는 찡그린 얼굴, 두 번째에는 담담한 얼굴. 자동차 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Anyone who pays you keeps a fairness ledger.
body: The rule applies to employees judging pay cuts, tenants judging rent and other departments judging what an internal team charges them.
In every case, people ask the same question: is this protecting your normal position, or grabbing more because I can't easily leave?
cards.softwareNote: Software users react the same way. A price rise that comes with clear new costs or features is tolerated. Raising seat prices right after customers have migrated their data and can't easily switch reads as a lock-in grab, and churn often follows at renewal.

cards.title: Fairness is a perception, so it has limits.
body: Explaining costs only works if it's true. Customers who later discover a "cost increase" was invented feel doubly cheated.
Norms also shift. Airline and hotel buyers now expect prices to move with demand, because those prices always have. A new swing in a market used to stable prices triggers the strongest backlash.
And fairness doesn't cancel economics. Holding prices down in a shortage can mean long queues or no service at all.

cards.title: Now you run an internal data team.
body: Your team runs the company's analytics platform and charges other departments $40 per user each month. The software vendor has just raised your license cost 25%. You'd also like money for a new project.
How do you set next year's internal rate?

options.text: Move to $50, show the vendor increase, and give three months' notice
options.feedback: The rise matches a real cost and arrives with warning. Departments may grumble, but they'll see you protecting your budget, not padding it.

options.text: Jump to $60 to cover the vendor and fund the new project
options.feedback: You get the funding, but other teams can see the vendor news too. A rise beyond it looks like taxing a captive customer, and they may push to buy their own tools.

options.text: Absorb the cost this year and catch up with a bigger rise next year
options.feedback: Calm for now, but a large later jump with no fresh cost behind it looks arbitrary. Small, explained moves usually land better.

cards.title: Customers judge the reason, not just the price.
body: Price rises tied to real costs are usually forgiven. Rises tied to a customer's urgency or lack of options are remembered.
**Try it today:** take your next planned price change and write the one-sentence reason you'd give a customer. If you'd hesitate to say it out loud, rethink the change.
